domains.title: Dangun, the Sandalwood Prince
domains.subtitle: founder of Gojoseon and first ancestor of the Korean people
domains.lead: Dangun is the legendary founder of Gojoseon and the first ancestor of the Korean people in Korean tradition. The name means "Lord of the sandalwood" and belongs to the domain "Founder of Korea, First King." Dangun is the son of Hwanung, the heavenly prince who descended to earth, and Ungnyeo, a bear who became a woman after enduring one hundred days in a cave eating garlic and mugwort. He is said to have founded the state of Gojoseon at Asadal in 2333 BCE, an event commemorated on National Foundation Day, 3 October.

cards.name: Founder of Gojoseon
cards.desc: Dangun is the mythic first king whose reign marks the beginning of Korean statehood.

cards.name: Son of Hwanung and Ungnyeo
cards.desc: His birth unites heavenly descent with the transformed earth-animal, modelling cosmic and terrestrial harmony.

cards.name: Asadal
cards.desc: The sacred capital where Dangun established law, agriculture, and the ordering of the people.

cards.name: Sansin
cards.desc: After his long reign Dangun became a mountain spirit, still invoked for protection and prosperity.

symbols.name: The sandalwood tree
symbols.meaning: Dang 檀 means sandalwood; the tree marks the sacred descent place of Hwanung.

symbols.name: Bear and tiger
symbols.meaning: The two animals who underwent Hwanung's trial; the bear's perseverance became the origin of the Korean people.

symbols.name: Garlic and mugwort
symbols.meaning: The austere foods of transformation, marking the passage from animal to human and from wilderness to culture.

symbols.name: Mountain peak
symbols.meaning: The place where Dangun withdrew and continues to dwell as a protective mountain spirit.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Dangun is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Bear and the Tiger
myths.text: Hwanung tested a bear and a tiger by locking them in a cave with only garlic and mugwort. The tiger gave up, but the bear endured one hundred days and became a woman named Ungnyeo. Hwanung then took her as his wife, and she bore Dangun.

myths.title: The Founding of Gojoseon
myths.text: Dangun established the capital at Asadal and ruled over Gojoseon for one thousand five hundred years. The date traditionally given for the founding, 3 October 2333 BCE, is celebrated as National Foundation Day.

myths.title: Dangun Becomes Mountain Spirit
myths.text: At the end of his reign Dangun left the affairs of state and withdrew into the mountains, where he became a sansin, a mountain deity who continues to protect the land and its people.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 檀 (dang, "sandalwood") with 君 (gun, "prince, lord, ruler"). The sandalwood tree is the axis mundi of the founding myth; the title gun marks Dangun as the first legitimate ruler.

nameVariations.note: Hanja form used in classical texts.

originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Dangun, the Hangul form is 단군 and the Hanja form is 檀君. Hangul ‘단군’ and Hanja ‘檀君’, attested in the Samguk Yusa and Samguk Sagi. The ASCII form dangun is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Dangun is the scholarly citation form.
syncretism: The Dangun myth has been interpreted through many lenses: as a nativist charter myth, as a Confucian parable of virtuous rule, as a Buddhist tale of miraculous birth, and, in the modern era, as a national foundation narrative. North and South Korea both claim Dangun as a common ancestor, though their political interpretations differ. The myth also resonates with broader northeast Asian stories of bear ancestors and celestial founders.
culturalLegacy: Dangun is perhaps the most potent symbol of Korean national identity. His tomb near Pyongyang, the annual Gaecheonjeol ceremony, and countless school textbooks, monuments, and cultural productions keep the figure present in public life. The story is also invoked by overseas Korean communities and by inter-Korean dialogue that seeks a shared mythic past. In popular culture Dangun appears in films, video games, and webtoons, often reimagined as a heroic founder.
extendedMeditation: Dangun invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
